stem: A model achieves 98% training accuracy but 62% test accuracy. This is most likely:
explanation_after: A large gap between training accuracy (98%) and test accuracy (62%) is the classic signature of overfitting — the model has memorised training patterns that don't generalise to new data.

stem: A model achieves 62% training accuracy and 60% test accuracy. This is most likely:
explanation_after: When both training and test accuracy are equally low, there's no generalisation gap — the model is underfitting. It hasn't learned the underlying pattern at all, performing badly everywhere.

stem: On the training loss curve, overfitting begins when:

options.text: Validation loss starts increasing while training loss continues to decrease
Training loss and validation loss are equal

explanation_after: Overfitting starts when the model starts to memorise training data. The validation loss stops improving and begins to rise while training loss continues to fall — this is the divergence point.

stem: Which technique specifically addresses overfitting by randomly disabling neurons during training?
explanation_after: Dropout randomly zeroes out a fraction of neurons during each training step, preventing any single neuron from being relied upon and forcing distributed representations. This reduces overfitting.

stem: L1 regularisation (Lasso) is distinct from L2 regularisation (Ridge) because:

options.text: L1 penalises squared weights while L2 penalises absolute weights
L1 drives some weights to exactly zero, performing feature selection
L1 works only for classification while L2 works for regression

explanation_after: L1 penalises the sum of absolute values of weights. Its gradient is constant (not proportional to weight size), which causes small weights to become exactly zero — performing automatic feature selection.

options.text: Stopping training before the model learns anything
Stopping training when validation loss stops improving, to prevent memorisation of training data
Reducing the learning rate over time

explanation_after: Early stopping monitors validation loss and stops training when it plateaus or starts increasing. The model is restored to the checkpoint with the best validation loss — the optimal point before overfitting.

stem: A model overfits with L2 regularisation strength set very low (train 96%, test 78%). The team increases the regularisation strength dramatically to 'fix' it, and now the model scores only 61% on both train and test. What happened?

options.text: The stronger regularisation successfully fixed overfitting, and this is the ideal outcome
The regularisation strength was pushed too far, and the model now underfits — regularisation strength needs to be tuned, not maximised
The test set must have changed between the two training runs
L2 regularisation stops having any effect once its strength exceeds a small threshold

explanation_after: Regularisation strength is a dial to balance, not a lever to maximise. Too little allowed the model to memorise training data (overfitting); too much constrains the model so heavily it can no longer fit even the training data (underfitting). The goal is finding a middle value where validation performance is best.

stem: For a model overfitting a small dataset, which fix most directly addresses the root cause rather than just constraining the symptom?

options.text: Collecting more diverse training data, so the model can no longer simply memorise a small, limited sample

explanation_after: Regularisation techniques like dropout and L2 make memorisation harder, but they don't change the underlying problem: too little data to characterise the true pattern. More diverse training data directly reduces how much the model can memorise, since there's more genuine signal and less of a small fixed sample to overfit to — it's often the single most effective fix, though it isn't always feasible, which is why regularisation is used as a practical alternative.
